name: Laser genesis

lead: Laser Genesis is a brand name for a low-energy 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser treatment that clinics offer for skin tone, redness and fine lines. It is usually described as a gentle option with little downtime.

The infrared light passes through the surface and warms the dermis without removing the epidermis; providers say this prompts collagen remodeling and less visible redness. Published research on it for appearance is sparse: one randomized split-face trial in eight people compared it with grid fractional radiofrequency for wrinkles around the eyes, and other registered studies are small.

paras: It is done in a clinic, usually as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart, with people returning to normal activity right away. Results are described as gradual improvements in tone and texture.

Nd:YAG lasers at 1064 nm carry an eye-injury hazard because the beam is invisible, so eye protection is used. Cosmetic adverse-event rates for this specific treatment were not found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Laser Genesis warms the dermis with a gentle 1064-nm laser, which providers say calms redness and refines texture for smoother, more even skin with little downtime. Published appearance data are limited to a small split-face trial and registered studies.

lead: Laser Genesis is the name of a non-ablative skin treatment that uses a long-pulsed 1064-nm neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Nd:YAG) laser at low energy. It is marketed for improving skin tone, redness and fine texture and is often described as a gentle, low-downtime option. A split-face trial refers to it as the 1064-nm long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser known as Laser Genesis [1].

The Nd:YAG laser medium emits infrared light at 1064 nm, which is weakly absorbed by water-rich tissue and is used in medicine for hair removal, minor vascular lesions and other dermatologic applications [2].

Published evidence specific to Laser Genesis for appearance is small: one randomized split-face study compared it with grid fractional radiofrequency for periorbital wrinkles in eight patients [1], and several small registered studies of 1064-nm devices exist [3][4].
infobox: Varies by device; not assessed here

paras: Nd:YAG lasers are solid-state lasers whose main output is invisible infrared light at 1064 nm. Because the wavelength is poorly absorbed by water, it can reach beneath the skin surface, and the same laser type is used for hair removal, small facial or leg vessels and other procedures [2].

Clinics that offer Laser Genesis describe delivering repeated low-energy pulses to warm the dermis without damaging the surface, with the aim of changing the look of redness, pore size and fine lines. Registered studies of other 1064-nm non-ablative devices have addressed photoaging and pigmentation [4].

A randomized, single-blind, split-face prospective study in Filipino patients (eight participants with moderate to severe periorbital wrinkles) compared grid fractional monopolar radiofrequency with the 1064-nm Laser Genesis. Its authors noted that controlled head-to-head comparisons of the two had been lacking [1].

Several small studies registered on ClinicalTrials.gov have tested Cutera-type Genesis or 1064-nm devices. These include a 17-person open-label study of 1064 nm for non-ablative rejuvenation in photoaging and pigmentation [4], a 20-person evaluation of a Cutera Excel V laser with a Green Genesis setting for wrinkles, rosacea and scarring [3], a 9-person study of a non-ablative laser for brow-lift scars [5], and a 100-patient chart review of a GenesisPlus laser for toenail fungus [6]. Registry entries do not by themselves report outcomes.

The Nd:YAG literature notes eye injury as the principal hazard of 1064-nm lasers because the beam is invisible [2]. Specific adverse-event rates for Laser Genesis in cosmetic use are not reported in the sources reviewed here.
